title: Jeremiah Chapter 24 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Jeremiah chapter 24 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Jeremiah Chapter 24 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Jeremiah Chapter 24.

questions.question: What did the LORD show Jeremiah in his vision?
options: Two baskets of figs set before the temple of the LORD
A river flowing from the temple
A lion roaring at the city gates
questions.correctAnswer: Two baskets of figs set before the temple of the LORD
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1 states that the LORD showed Jeremiah two baskets of figs set before the temple of the LORD.

questions.question: Who had carried away captive Jeconiah and the princes of Judah?
questions.correctAnswer: Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1 specifies that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon carried away captive Jeconiah and the princes of Judah.

questions.question: Along with the princes of Judah, who else was carried away captive to Babylon?
questions.correctAnswer: Carpenters and smiths
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1 mentions that carpenters and smiths were also taken captive along with the princes of Judah.

questions.question: How were the figs in the first basket described?
options: Very good, like figs that are first ripe
questions.correctAnswer: Very good, like figs that are first ripe
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:2 describes one basket having very good figs, like the figs that are first ripe.

questions.question: How were the figs in the second basket described?
options: Very naughty, so bad they could not be eaten
questions.correctAnswer: Very naughty, so bad they could not be eaten
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:2 says the other basket had very naughty figs which could not be eaten because they were so bad.

questions.question: What did the LORD ask Jeremiah when He showed him the baskets of figs?
options: Who is worthy to eat these figs?
Will you plant these figs in the land?
How many figs are in each basket?
questions.correctAnswer: What seest thou, Jeremiah?
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:3 records that the LORD asked Jeremiah, 'What seest thou, Jeremiah?'.

questions.question: How did Jeremiah describe the figs to the LORD?
options: The good figs, very good; and the evil, very evil
The figs were sour and bitter
Only the good figs were visible
questions.correctAnswer: The good figs, very good; and the evil, very evil
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:3 states that Jeremiah described the figs as good figs, very good; and the evil figs, very evil.

questions.question: True or False: Jeremiah saw baskets of grapes in his vision instead of figs.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1-3 clearly states that Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs, not grapes.

questions.question: True or False: The good figs represented those carried away captive of Judah for their good.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:5 says the good figs symbolize those taken captive whom the LORD sent for their good.

questions.question: True or False: The LORD said the evil figs could be eaten if they were cooked.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:2-3 states the evil figs could not be eaten because they were so bad, with no mention of cooking.

questions.question: Which group does the LORD compare to the evil figs?
options: Zedekiah the king of Judah and his princes
Jeconiah and the princes taken to Babylon
questions.correctAnswer: Zedekiah the king of Judah and his princes
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:8 compares Zedekiah and his princes to the evil figs which could not be eaten.

questions.question: What happened after the LORD showed the baskets of figs to Jeremiah?
options: The word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah again
The baskets were taken away by Nebuchadrezzar
Jeremiah was commanded to plant the figs
questions.correctAnswer: The word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah again
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:4 states that again the word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah after the vision.

questions.question: In Jeremiah 24, which event happens first?
options: The LORD shows Jeremiah the two baskets of figs
The LORD gives Jeremiah the interpretation of the figs
The word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah again
Jeremiah is commanded to write a letter
questions.correctAnswer: The LORD shows Jeremiah the two baskets of figs
questions.explanation: According to Jeremiah 24:1, first the LORD showed Jeremiah the two baskets of figs before giving further words.

questions.question: What did Jeremiah say about the evil figs when asked by the LORD?
options: They are so evil, they cannot be eaten
They are just ripe and sweet
They look like the first ripe figs
questions.correctAnswer: They are so evil, they cannot be eaten
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:3 shows Jeremiah saying the evil figs are so evil they cannot be eaten.

questions.question: True or False: The vision of the two baskets of figs was shown to Jeremiah after the captivity of Jeconiah and others.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1 states that the vision occurred after Nebuchadrezzar had carried away Jeconiah and others captive.

medium.title: Jeremiah Chapter 24 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Jeremiah Chapter 24 to real-life situations.

questions.question: What did the LORD show Jeremiah in vision before the temple?
questions.correctAnswer: Two baskets of figs
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1 states that the LORD showed Jeremiah two baskets of figs set before the temple.

questions.question: How are the two baskets of figs described?
options: One basket had good figs, the other had very bad figs
Both baskets had very good figs
One basket had sour figs, the other sweet figs
questions.correctAnswer: One basket had good figs, the other had very bad figs
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:2 describes one basket containing very good figs, like first ripe figs, and the other basket containing very bad figs that could not be eaten.

questions.question: What was Jeremiah's response when asked what he saw?
options: He saw good figs and evil figs, very evil and uneatable
He saw a field of wheat
questions.correctAnswer: He saw good figs and evil figs, very evil and uneatable
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:3 records Jeremiah saying he saw good figs, very good, and evil figs, very evil, which could not be eaten.

questions.question: What does the LORD say about the good figs in relation to the captives of Judah?
options: He will acknowledge and care for them
questions.correctAnswer: He will acknowledge and care for them
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:5 explains that like the good figs, the LORD will acknowledge those carried captive of Judah and sent into the land of the Chaldeans for their good.

questions.question: According to Jeremiah 24:6, what will God do for those carried captive?
options: He will set His eyes upon them for good and bring them back to their land
He will make them wander endlessly
He will punish them with exile
questions.correctAnswer: He will set His eyes upon them for good and bring them back to their land
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:6 states that God will set His eyes upon them for good, bring them back, build them, and plant them in their land without uprooting.

questions.question: How will God change the hearts of the captives according to Jeremiah 24:7?
options: He will give them a heart to know Him and they will return with their whole heart
He will harden their hearts against Him
He will make them forget Him
He will give them a heart to rebel
questions.correctAnswer: He will give them a heart to know Him and they will return with their whole heart
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:7 promises that God will give them a heart to know Him so they will return and be His people.

questions.question: Who are represented by the "evil figs" in the vision?
options: Zedekiah the king of Judah, his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem remaining in the land
questions.correctAnswer: Zedekiah the king of Judah, his princes, and the residue of Jerusalem remaining in the land
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:8 identifies the evil figs as Zedekiah, his princes, the people remaining in the land, and those in Egypt.

questions.question: What will happen to those likened to the evil figs according to Jeremiah 24:9?
options: They will be removed into all kingdoms to be a reproach and curse
They will be honored and blessed
They will build a great kingdom
They will be protected from harm
questions.correctAnswer: They will be removed into all kingdoms to be a reproach and curse
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:9 states that those like the evil figs will be scattered into all kingdoms and become a reproach, proverb, taunt, and curse.

questions.question: What three calamities will God send upon the evil figs until they are consumed, as per Jeremiah 24:10?
questions.correctAnswer: Sword, famine, and pestilence
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:10 declares that God will send sword, famine, and pestilence among them until they are consumed from the land.

questions.question: How does Jeremiah 24:5-7 teach us about God's faithfulness to those who are captive?
options: God watches over them for good and will restore them with a changed heart
Captivity means permanent judgment without hope
God's faithfulness is limited to the land only
questions.correctAnswer: God watches over them for good and will restore them with a changed heart
questions.explanation: Verses 5-7 show God acknowledging captives for their good, promising restoration, rebuilding, planting, and giving them a heart to know Him and return fully.

questions.question: What biblical truth can be applied when a believer feels rejected like the captives in Babylon?
options: God sees them for good and will restore them with a new heart
They are permanently forsaken without hope
They should isolate from God and others
They must earn God's favor by deeds
questions.correctAnswer: God sees them for good and will restore them with a new heart
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:6-7 teaches that God sets His eyes on the captives for good, promises restoration, and gives them a heart to know Him and return fully.

questions.question: According to Jeremiah 24:8-10, what is the consequence for those who reject God’s ways?
options: They will be scattered and suffer sword, famine, and pestilence
They will receive mercy and restoration
They will be exalted among nations
They will live in peace and prosperity
questions.correctAnswer: They will be scattered and suffer sword, famine, and pestilence
questions.explanation: Verses 8-10 describe how those like evil figs will be removed into all kingdoms for harm and will experience sword, famine, and pestilence until destroyed.

questions.question: True or False? Jeremiah’s vision implies that God differentiates between those who obey Him and those who rebel.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:5-10 uses the metaphor of good and evil figs to distinguish between those God acknowledges and restores, and those He punishes for rebellion.

questions.question: True or False? The vision of the two baskets of figs was shown after the captivity of Jeconiah and the princes.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1 specifies the vision occurred after Nebuchadrezzar carried away Jeconiah and the princes to Babylon.

questions.question: True or False? According to Jeremiah 24, all the people of Judah will be restored to their land regardless of their heart condition.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:5-7 contrasts those carried captive who will be restored with a heart to know God, and those remaining who will face judgment (24:8-10), showing restoration depends on heart condition.

hard.title: Jeremiah Chapter 24 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Jeremiah Chapter 24.

questions.question: According to Jeremiah 24, what will happen to those who remain in the land of Judah and Egypt, described as the "evil figs"?
options: They will be restored to the land and prosper
They will be removed into all kingdoms of the earth for their hurt
They will build new temples and cities
They will become kings and priests
questions.correctAnswer: They will be removed into all kingdoms of the earth for their hurt
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:9 states that the evil figs, representing those remaining in Judah and Egypt, will be delivered to all the kingdoms of the earth for their hurt, becoming a reproach and a curse.

questions.question: What three calamities does the LORD say He will send among the people until they are consumed from the land?
questions.correctAnswer: Sword, famine, and pestilence
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:10 explicitly mentions the sword, famine, and pestilence as the means God will use to consume the people from the land He gave to them and their fathers.

questions.question: In Jeremiah 24, what is the significance of the two baskets of figs shown to Jeremiah?
options: They represent two groups of people: those taken captive and those who remain
They symbolize two different kingdoms fighting
They show the difference between harvests in Judah and Babylon
They depict the difference between good and evil kings
questions.correctAnswer: They represent two groups of people: those taken captive and those who remain
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1-3 explains that the good figs represent the captives taken to Babylon, and the evil figs represent those who remain in Judah and Egypt, symbolizing God's judgment and mercy.

questions.question: What promise does God make concerning the captives represented by the good figs?
options: He will set His eyes upon them for good and bring them back to the land
He will make them kings over other nations
questions.correctAnswer: He will set His eyes upon them for good and bring them back to the land
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:5-6 promises that God will look upon the captives for good, bring them back, build and plant them in the land rather than pull them up.

questions.question: What heart does God say He will give to the captives, according to Jeremiah 24?
options: A heart to know God and return to Him wholly
A heart indifferent to their past
questions.correctAnswer: A heart to know God and return to Him wholly
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:7 states that God will give the captives a heart to know Him so that they will be His people and return to Him with their whole heart.

questions.question: True or False: According to Jeremiah 24, those carried away captive to Babylon are described as 'evil figs' that cannot be eaten because they are so bad.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:2-3 distinguishes the good figs as those taken captive to Babylon (the good group) and the evil figs as those remaining in Judah and Egypt; the captives are the good figs, not the evil.

questions.question: Which king is specifically mentioned as being given over like the 'evil figs'?
questions.correctAnswer: Zedekiah
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:8 names Zedekiah the king of Judah as one who, with his princes and people, will be like the evil figs, facing removal and judgment.

questions.question: Which Old Testament passage echoes the theme of exile and restoration found in Jeremiah 24?
questions.correctAnswer: Isaiah 11:11-12
questions.explanation: Isaiah 11:11-12 discusses the future gathering and restoration of Israel from exile, paralleling Jeremiah 24's promise of return for the captives (cf. Jeremiah 24:6-7).

questions.question: What literary device is used in Jeremiah 24 through the contrasting baskets of figs to convey God’s message?
questions.correctAnswer: Allegory
questions.explanation: The two baskets of figs serve as an allegory in Jeremiah 24:1-3, representing two groups of people and their differing fates under God's judgment and mercy.

questions.question: What is the Hebrew meaning of the word translated as 'pestilence' in Jeremiah 24:10, and what does it imply in this context?
options: A contagious disease causing widespread death
A natural disaster like an earthquake
questions.correctAnswer: A contagious disease causing widespread death
questions.explanation: The Hebrew word "dever" (דֶּבֶר), translated as 'pestilence' in Jeremiah 24:10, denotes a deadly plague or contagious disease, underscoring the severity of God's judgment on those remaining in the land.

questions.question: Which New Testament passage reflects the theme of God's people being scattered among the nations as a reproach, similar to Jeremiah 24?
questions.explanation: John 15:18-21 reflects on the disciples being hated and scattered by the world, echoing Jeremiah 24:9’s theme of God’s people becoming a reproach and taunt among the nations.

questions.question: How does Jeremiah 24 display a theme of hope amid judgment that is also foundational in the book of Ezekiel?
options: Through the promise of a new covenant
Through the vision of dry bones coming to life
Through the promise of return and a heart to know God
Through the prophecy of a new temple
questions.correctAnswer: Through the promise of return and a heart to know God
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:7 promises God will give the captives a heart to know Him, paralleling Ezekiel 36:26-27 where God promises a new heart and spirit, emphasizing restoration amid judgment.

questions.question: According to Jeremiah 24, what is the authorial intent behind showing Jeremiah the two baskets of figs?
options: To reveal the economic condition of Judah
To illustrate the fate of two groups of Judah's people under God’s judgment and mercy
To prophesy the fall of Babylon
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate the fate of two groups of Judah's people under God’s judgment and mercy
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:4-5 clarifies that the vision was to show the fate of those taken captive (good figs) and those remaining (evil figs), conveying God’s judgment and promise of restoration.

questions.question: True or False: Jeremiah 24 describes the removal of the people as a blessing and a sign of God's favor.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:9-10 shows that the removal of the wicked is for their hurt and as a curse, involving sword, famine, and pestilence, not a blessing or favor.

questions.question: In Jeremiah 24, how is the concept of divine retribution expressed through the fate of the 'evil figs'?
options: They will receive wealth and honor
They will be made rulers over other nations
They will be a reproach, proverb, taunt, and curse in all places
They will be forgiven without punishment
questions.correctAnswer: They will be a reproach, proverb, taunt, and curse in all places
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:9 describes how the 'evil figs' will be scattered and become a reproach and curse wherever they are driven, highlighting the theme of divine judgment.

theological.title: Jeremiah Chapter 24 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Jeremiah Chapter 24 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What do the two baskets of figs represent in Jeremiah 24?
options: The exiles who will prosper and those who will suffer judgment
The kings of Judah and Babylon
The land of Judah and the land of Egypt
questions.correctAnswer: The exiles who will prosper and those who will suffer judgment
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1-2 explains that the two baskets of figs symbolize two groups of people: the good figs represent the captives taken to Babylon whom God will bless, and the bad figs represent those who remain in Judah or flee to Egypt who will face judgment.

questions.question: According to Jeremiah 24:5, what is God's purpose in sending the captives to Babylon?
questions.correctAnswer: For their good
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:5 explicitly states that God acknowledges those carried captive to Babylon for their good, indicating a divine purpose of restoration and blessing despite their exile.

questions.question: Which doctrine is illustrated by Jeremiah 24:6 in God's promise to the exiles?
options: The doctrine of divine restoration and covenant faithfulness
questions.correctAnswer: The doctrine of divine restoration and covenant faithfulness
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:6 affirms God's promise to rebuild and plant the exiles rather than uproot them, demonstrating His covenant faithfulness and restorative grace toward His people.

questions.question: What attribute of God is revealed in Jeremiah 24:7 where He gives the captives 'an heart to know me'?
questions.correctAnswer: Grace and sovereignty in regeneration
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:7 shows God's sovereign grace in regenerating hearts so that the people come to know Him and return wholeheartedly, highlighting His role in spiritual renewal.

questions.question: According to Jeremiah 24:8, who are represented by the 'evil figs' that cannot be eaten?
options: Zedekiah, his princes, and the remnant in Judah and Egypt
questions.correctAnswer: Zedekiah, his princes, and the remnant in Judah and Egypt
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:8 identifies the evil figs as Zedekiah, the princes, and those remaining in Judah and Egypt, who will experience judgment for their disobedience.

questions.question: What does Jeremiah 24:9 teach about the consequences awaiting the 'evil figs'?
options: They will be honored and restored
They will be scattered and become a taunt and curse among nations
questions.correctAnswer: They will be scattered and become a taunt and curse among nations
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:9 states that the evil figs will be removed to all kingdoms of the earth for harm and will become a proverb and curse, illustrating the judgment and disgrace they will face.

questions.question: How does Jeremiah 24:10 depict God's justice upon those who reject Him?
options: By sending sword, famine, and pestilence until they are consumed
questions.correctAnswer: By sending sword, famine, and pestilence until they are consumed
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:10 describes God's just judgment through sending sword, famine, and pestilence to consume those who reject Him, showing the severity of divine wrath against unrepentance.

questions.question: What combined doctrine is taught by Jeremiah 24:5-6 and 24:7 about God's actions toward the exiles?
options: God's sovereign restoration and regeneration of His people
questions.correctAnswer: God's sovereign restoration and regeneration of His people
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:5-6 and 24:7 together reveal that God not only restores the exiles physically to their land but also regenerates their hearts, demonstrating His sovereign work in both temporal and spiritual restoration.

questions.question: Sceptics claim that God’s sending the captives to Babylon proves He is unjust. What does Jeremiah 24:5-7 actually teach about God's justice and mercy?
options: God punishes without purpose or hope
God’s discipline serves a redemptive purpose and includes mercy and restoration
God is indifferent to human suffering
questions.correctAnswer: God’s discipline serves a redemptive purpose and includes mercy and restoration
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:5-7 teaches that God’s sending of captives is for their good, involving discipline that leads to restoration and a renewed relationship with Him, affirming His justice and mercy working together (cf. Hebrews 12:6).

questions.question: How does the imagery in Jeremiah 24 contribute to the biblical theology of exile and restoration?
options: It denies the possibility of return from exile
It foreshadows the ultimate restoration through the Messiah
It focuses only on political events
It emphasizes human strength over divine grace
questions.correctAnswer: It foreshadows the ultimate restoration through the Messiah
questions.explanation: The good figs symbolize God's people who will be restored, pointing forward to the ultimate restoration in Christ who gathers His people from exile, aligning with the biblical theme of redemption (cf. Isaiah 11:11-12).

questions.question: What attribute of God is demonstrated by His promise in Jeremiah 24:6 to 'build and not pull down' the exiles?
questions.correctAnswer: God’s faithfulness and steadfast love
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:6 reveals God’s faithful commitment to His covenant people, showing His loving purpose to restore and not destroy, reflecting His steadfast love (cf. Lamentations 3:22-23).

questions.question: What theological insight emerges from comparing the fate of the 'good figs' and 'evil figs' in Jeremiah 24?
options: All are equally blessed by God
God’s judgment and mercy are distinct and purposeful
questions.correctAnswer: God’s judgment and mercy are distinct and purposeful
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24 contrasts the good figs (to be restored) with the evil figs (to be judged), illustrating God’s righteous distinction in dealing with His people according to their faithfulness and obedience.

questions.question: What narrative arc connection does Jeremiah 24 make with the broader story of Israel’s redemption?
options: It depicts Israel’s final destruction without hope
It reveals God’s ongoing plan to restore His people despite judgment
It focuses solely on secular history
questions.correctAnswer: It reveals God’s ongoing plan to restore His people despite judgment
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24 fits into the redemptive narrative by showing exile as a form of divine discipline followed by promised restoration, consistent with God’s covenant faithfulness throughout Scripture (cf. Deuteronomy 30:3-5).

questions.question: What does Jeremiah 24:1 indicate about the historical context of the vision of the two baskets of figs?
options: It occurred before the Babylonian exile
It occurred after Nebuchadnezzar’s captivity of Jeconiah and the princes
It took place during the reign of King David
It was unrelated to any historical event
questions.correctAnswer: It occurred after Nebuchadnezzar’s captivity of Jeconiah and the princes
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:1 situates the vision after Nebuchadnezzar had taken Jeconiah, the princes, carpenters, and smiths captive to Babylon, grounding the vision within a specific historical exile event.

questions.question: Which doctrine is underscored by Jeremiah 24:9’s depiction of the exiles becoming 'a reproach and a proverb' among nations?
options: The doctrine of divine judgment and the consequences of sin
The doctrine of predestination without human responsibility
questions.correctAnswer: The doctrine of divine judgment and the consequences of sin
questions.explanation: Jeremiah 24:9 emphasizes that God's judgment leads to public reproach and dispersion, underscoring the biblical teaching that sin brings consequences and divine justice is manifested visibly.
